concepts.title: Conveying the main idea with a simple example
concepts.one_liner: A paper should include a simple example that captures its main idea and highlights the specific problem or drawback being addressed.
concepts.content: A paper should include an example that captures its main idea. For instance, a figure can convey a core concept very simply, such as demonstrating how a specific representation lacks desirable features. (see figure: Effect of translation on the wavelet representation of a signal (caption and figure after @Simoncelli92. (a) An input signal. (b-d) The high-, mid-, and low-frequency coefficients within a wavelet...) In the case of wavelet representations, a figure can show the failure to form a translation-invariant representation. By showing two versions of the same signal differing only by a one-sample translation, the figure points out the drawback of aliased subbands: as the signal translates, the representation energy moves to different frequency bands and changes form.
concepts.motivation_md: Complex technical arguments can be difficult to grasp quickly. A simple, well-chosen example or figure allows the reader to immediately understand the core problem and the paper's primary contribution.
concepts.recap_md: - Use a simple example to capture the paper's main idea and core contribution.

concepts.title: Standards for experimental results
concepts.one_liner: Modern research standards require that all assertions in a paper be backed up with quantitative experimental evidence and comparisons to the state-of-the-art.
concepts.content: Modern standards require that assertions in a paper be backed up with experimental evidence. Readers will expect a table quantitatively comparing the performance of your algorithm with that of the previous state-of-the-art. If you are proposing a new task for which there aren't previous benchmarks, you should still compare with an algorithm that solves a related task, noting that the algorithm was designed for a different task. (see figure: prototypical table of results, from \cite{Owens2016} Rows are different algorithms, or ablations of a favored algorithm. Columns are datasets or tasks, and the numbers indicate performance, with the...)
concepts.motivation_md: Plausibility arguments are no longer sufficient in computer vision; quantitative evidence is necessary to prove that a new method actually improves upon existing work.
concepts.recap_md: - Back up all claims with quantitative experimental evidence.

concepts.title: How to (and how not to) end a paper
concepts.one_liner: A paper should conclude by reviewing contributions and new research directions rather than listing unfinished work.
concepts.content: You should resist the temptation to describe items that were left unfinished in a section on "Future Work." It is a weak way to end a paper by enumerating all the things the paper doesn't accomplish or providing a summary of where it falls short. Instead, the paper can finish with a review of what has been presented, emphasizing the contributions. Address how the world has changed now that the reader has read the paper, what new research directions have been opened up, and what can be done now that couldn't be done before.
concepts.motivation_md: Ending on unfinished work highlights weaknesses. Ending on contributions reinforces the value of the research and its impact on the field.
concepts.recap_md: - Avoid ending with a list of unfinished "Future Work."

key_passage.text: Instead, the paper can finish with a review what has been presented, emphasizing the contributions. How has the world changed, now that the reader has read this paper? What new research directions have been opened up; what can we do now that we couldn't do before?

motivation.text: It is hard to imagine a weaker way to end the paper than to enumerate all the things the paper doesn't accomplish, providing a summary of where it falls short.

concepts.title: Keep the reader uppermost in mind
concepts.one_liner: The most important principle of good writing is to anticipate the reader's knowledge and expectations at every step.
concepts.content: Perhaps the most important principle of good writing is to keep the reader uppermost in mind: What does the reader know so far? What does the reader expect next and why? The ideal writer acts like a great host who anticipates every need of their guest, knowing at every moment what the reader might be wanting and how to help them find it.
concepts.motivation_md: Writing is an act of communication; if the author does not account for the reader's perspective, the technical content may become inaccessible or confusing.
concepts.recap_md: - Constantly ask what the reader knows and what they expect next.

key_passage.text: Perhaps the most important principle of good writing is to keep the reader uppermost in mind: What does the reader know so far? What does the reader expect next and why?

concepts.title: The importance of concise writing
concepts.one_liner: Vigorous writing is concise, containing no unnecessary words or sentences to ensure clarity and fit within page limits.
concepts.content: Vigorous writing is concise. A sentence should contain no unnecessary words and a paragraph no unnecessary sentences. Writing more concisely helps a paper in two ways. First, researchers often face strict page limits, particularly in conference submissions; tighter text allows the author to say more or include additional figures. Second, concise text is usually clearer and easier for the reader to understand. For example, a technical paragraph can often be reduced significantly in length (e.g., from 149 words to 88 words) without changing its meaning, simply by removing roundabout descriptions.
concepts.motivation_md: Conciseness respects the reader's time and maximizes the information density allowed by strict publication constraints.
concepts.recap_md: - Remove unnecessary words and sentences to improve clarity.

key_passage.text: Vigorous writing is concise. A sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences, for the same reason that a drawing should have no unnecessary lines and a machine no unnecessary parts.

motivation.text: Note that writing more concise text helps your paper in two ways. First, researchers are typically fighting against a page limit, particularly in conference submissions, so tighter text lets the author say more or add another figure. Second, concise text is usually clearer and easier to understand.

concepts.title: Engagement levels of paper readers
concepts.one_liner: Since many readers only skim papers, the title, abstract, and figures should independently convey the paper's core message.
concepts.content: Most readers will probably only skim your paper rather than reading every word. Because of this, you should write your paper so that readers will learn from it even at reduced levels of engagement. The title should convey the top-level message of the paper. The abstract should provide a good summary, and the figures and their captions should be self-contained to tell the story of the paper. (see figure: The conjectured readership of a computer science paper (conjectured relative amounts). Many people will read the title, but far fewer will read the abstract or look at the figures. Fewer still will...)
concepts.motivation_md: In an era of high publication volume, authors must ensure their main contributions are accessible to skimmers who may never read the full text.
concepts.recap_md: - Ensure the title, abstract, and figures convey the main message independently.

concepts.title: Catchy titles and top-level messages
concepts.one_liner: A good title generates attention and interest by clearly stating the paper's main point or asking a compelling question.
concepts.content: A good title can generate attention and interest for a paper. Effective titles often let the reader see the delight or the main point of the work immediately, such as "What makes Paris look like Paris." While a technical title like "Shiftable Multi-scale Transforms" may be appropriate, adding a catchy subtitle or phrase that tells the main point—such as "What's wrong with wavelets?"—can make the paper much more engaging.
concepts.motivation_md: The title is the first thing a potential reader sees; a catchy title increases the likelihood that the paper will be noticed and read.
concepts.recap_md: - Use titles that generate interest and convey the main point immediately.

key_passage.text: A good title can generate attention and interest for the paper.

motivation.text: A good title can generate attention and interest for the paper. "What makes Paris look like Paris" is a delightful paper, and the title lets the reader see that right away. In contrast, one of us coauthored a paper called "Shiftable Multi-scale Transforms." While that title is appropriate, it's not catchy. After the paper was in print, we realized that we should have added the subtitle, "What's wrong with wavelets?" --- a catchy phrase that tells the main point of the paper.

concepts.title: Writing self-contained figure captions
concepts.one_liner: Figure captions should be self-contained and explicitly state what the reader is supposed to notice.
concepts.content: Because many readers of figure captions will not be reading the full paper, the captions should be self-contained. They should point out what readers are supposed to notice about the figure, helping both the full-paper reader and the figures-only reader understand the takeaway. (see figure: Figure and caption from \cite{FreemanShapetime}. The caption should be understandable by itself, and should point to what the reader should take away from the figure.)
concepts.motivation_md: Self-contained captions ensure that the visual evidence of a paper remains informative even when viewed in isolation from the main text.
concepts.recap_md: - Write captions that are understandable without reading the main text.

concepts.title: Only the good papers count
concepts.one_liner: Focus on producing high-quality research, as only the truly good papers significantly impact a career.
concepts.content: While the number of papers is a rough measure of productivity, experienced mentors and hiring committees find that only the good papers count. You should strive to make all your papers high-quality, as only the really good papers matter for your career. This relationship between quality and career impact is summarized in (see figure: Plot of conjectured data showing the impact of a paper on one's career, as a function of paper quality.). Consequently, it is essential to learn how to write the best possible paper from any given piece of research work.
concepts.motivation_md: Students often feel pressured to publish frequently, but long-term career success is driven by the depth and quality of contributions rather than sheer volume.
concepts.recap_md:
- Prioritize paper quality over quantity to maximize long-term career impact.
 - Recognize that influential research managers and faculty search committees value 'good' papers almost exclusively.
 - Invest time in learning how to communicate research effectively to ensure its quality is recognized.

concepts.title: Adelson's advice on paper organization
concepts.one_liner: Organize research papers by stating the problem, critiquing existing solutions, explaining your solution, and discussing related work.
concepts.content: Prof. Edward Adelson suggests a specific structure for writing a good paper: 1. Start by stating the problem and explaining why the audience should care about it. 2. Briefly state existing solutions and explain why they are unsatisfactory. 3. Explain your own solution, compare it with others, and demonstrate why it is better. 4. Conclude by discussing related work where similar techniques were applied to different problems. This structure aligns with typical conference paper headings, such as: Introduction, Related Work, Main Idea, Algorithm (including specific sub-steps like estimation or reconstruction), Experiments (covering various cases), and Discussion.
concepts.motivation_md: A clear, logical structure helps readers quickly grasp the value of a research contribution and follow the author's reasoning.
concepts.recap_md:
- Begin by defining the problem and establishing its importance to the reader.
 - Contrast your approach with existing solutions to justify the need for your work.
 - Use a standard progression of headings from introduction through experiments to discussion.

key_passage.text: Start by stating which problem you are addressing, keeping the audience in mind. Then state briefly what the other solutions are to the problem, and why they aren't satisfactory. Then explain your own solution, compare it with other solutions, and say why it's better. At the end, talk about related work where similar techniques and experiments have been used, but applied to a different problem.

concepts.title: Writing a dynamite introduction
concepts.one_liner: Write a 'dynamite' introduction that immediately clarifies the problem, the solution, the novelty, and the importance of the work.
concepts.content: Regarding paper introductions, Kajiya emphasizes the necessity of making a paper easy to read from the very beginning. You must write a 'dynamite introduction' that allows anyone to immediately understand what the paper is about, what problem it solves, why that problem is interesting, what is genuinely new versus what is not, and why the contribution is significant. All of this must be done up front.
concepts.motivation_md: The introduction is often the only part of a paper a reviewer or researcher reads thoroughly. It must successfully 'sell' the paper's value immediately.
concepts.recap_md:
- Ensure the introduction clearly states the problem, its interest, and your specific solution.
 - Explicitly distinguish what is new in your work from what is existing literature.
 - Make the paper's value proposition obvious 'up front' to engage the reader immediately.

motivation.text: You must make your paper easy to read. You've got to make it easy for anyone to tell what your paper is about, what problem it solves, why the problem is interesting, what is really new in your paper (and what isn't), why it's so neat.

concepts.title: Best practices for writing with equations
concepts.one_liner: Sentences should flow smoothly even when formulas are replaced by simple placeholder sounds, and equations should be identified by both phrase and number.
concepts.content: Equations interposed with text can pose a challenge to the reader, who must decide whether to stop to work through each equation or continue reading as if the equation were words. Knuth advises that because many readers skim formulas on a first reading, your sentences should flow smoothly when all but the simplest formulas are replaced by "blah" or some other grunting noise. Mermin adds that when referring to an equation, you should identify it by a phrase as well as a number. For example, instead of saying "inserting (2.47) and (3.51) into (5.13)," it is more helpful to say "inserting the form (2.47) of the electric field $E$ and the Lindhard form (3.51) of the dielectric function $\epsilon$ into the constitutive equation (5.13)."
concepts.motivation_md: Mathematical writing is often difficult to parse. These practices ensure that the narrative flow of a paper remains intact for skimmers while providing clear context for readers who are deeply analyzing the derivations.

concepts.title: Maintaining a generous and reliable tone
concepts.one_liner: Maintaining a generous, clear, and reliable tone wins over readers and builds a reputation for integrity in the research community.
concepts.content: The tone of your writing is important. While you may feel pressure to oversell your work, hide drawbacks, or disparage others, it is in your long-term interest to resist this. If your work has a shortcoming, it is better to point it out yourself than to have someone else do so later. Papers written from the perspective that researchers are all doing their best are much more pleasant to read than those that treat others as incompetent. A generous tone, such as acknowledging related independent work and urging readers to review it for a complete picture, wins over readers and promotes professional friendships. Furthermore, you should develop a reputation for being clear and reliable by conveying an accurate impression of an algorithm's performance. If a method fails in important cases, let the readers know; describing counterintuitive results or failures can prove valuable to the field later on.
concepts.motivation_md: Scientific progress relies on trust and collaboration. A generous and honest tone prevents future embarrassment, builds professional relationships, and ensures that the research community can accurately build upon your findings.

key_passage.text: Papers written from the point of view that "we're all good researchers, doing our best" are much more pleasant to read than papers written from the standpoint that everyone else is an idiot. This generous tone wins over the reader and promotes long-lasting friendships with people who study the same problems you do.

motivation.text: You should develop a reputation for being clear and reliable. Always convey an accurate impression of the performance of an algorithm.

concepts.title: Author List Best Practices
concepts.one_liner: The quality of a paper is more important than your specific position on the author list.
concepts.content: The quality of the papers you write matters much more than your positions within the author lists. If adding more authors will make a paper better, you should add them. If a collaborator feels they should be an author, but you are unsure, it is generally a good idea to trust the collaborator and add them as a coauthor. It is much better to be one of many authors on a great paper than to be one of just a few authors on a mediocre paper.
concepts.motivation_md: Collaboration often improves the depth and quality of research. Prioritizing the final output over individual ego or ranking fosters better science and healthier professional relationships.

concepts.title: Avoiding Paper Rejection
concepts.one_liner: To avoid paper rejection, ensure you deliver on promises, cite relevant work, provide believable results, and maintain high writing quality.
concepts.content: Conference area chairs often look for reasons to reject papers to manage high submission volumes. To avoid giving them easy reasons for rejection, ensure your paper addresses the following: Do the authors deliver what they promise? Are important references included to show the authors are current on the state of the art? Are the results more than just incremental? Are the results believable with sufficient tests to support claims? Is the paper well-written and free of mistakes or incorrect statements? Most decision-making effort goes into borderline papers, which can be categorized as either "cockroaches" or "puppies with six toes."
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the criteria and pressures faced by reviewers helps authors proactively address weaknesses that lead to quick rejections.

concepts.title: Cockroach Papers
concepts.one_liner: Cockroach papers are mundane submissions with incremental improvements and no exciting contributions that are difficult for reviewers to reject.
concepts.content:
"Cockroaches" have no exciting contributions, but the reviews are okay and the results show incremental improvement to the state of the art. They are hard to kill (hence the nickname); typically, two-thirds are accepted as posters and one-third are rejected. As an author, it is best to work harder for fresh results to move a paper out of this category.

concepts.motivation_md: This term identifies a specific type of borderline paper that lacks impact despite being technically sound, encouraging authors to strive for more significant contributions.

concepts.title: Puppy with Six Toes Papers
concepts.one_liner: Puppy with six toes papers are delightful and fresh works that are easily rejected due to a single, minor, but obvious flaw.
concepts.content:
"Puppies with six toes" are delightful papers that possess an easy-to-see flaw. The flaw may not truly matter—much like six toes on a puppy—but it makes the paper easy to reject even if the work is fresh and wonderful. Approximately two-thirds of these papers are rejected, while one-third may be accepted as posters. As an author, it may be better to wait for another submission cycle to remove the obvious flaw, which could lead to an oral presentation in the future.

prereq.rationale: Conciseness is a direct application of keeping the reader in mind, as it makes the text easier for them to understand.
Designing for skimmers requires anticipating the reader's behavior and needs at reduced levels of engagement.
Ensuring equations flow smoothly with text is a way to help the reader maintain their train of thought.
A generous and reliable tone is essential for winning over the reader and building long-term trust.
Believable results and sufficient tests are necessary to avoid easy rejection by area chairs.
Adelson's organizational structure is a primary method for ensuring a paper meets the quality standards required to have a meaningful impact in the research community.
The 'dynamite introduction' is a high-impact implementation of the first two steps in Adelson's paper structure: stating the problem and critiquing existing work.
Quantitative experimental evidence is the modern standard for the 'Experiments' and 'Algorithm' sections defined in Adelson's organizational framework.
The advice on concluding with contributions and new directions refines the 'Discussion' and 'Related Work' steps of the general paper organization.

overlay.rationale: Keeping the reader in mind is the foundational principle that informs the structural advice given by Adelson.
A catchy title is a specific technique to engage readers who are only skimming the top-level message.
Self-contained captions cater to the 'figures-only' reader, a specific level of readership engagement.
Cockroach papers represent a specific category of borderline papers that authors should try to avoid.
Puppy papers are fresh but flawed, whereas cockroach papers are mundane but solid.
Using a simple example or figure is a concrete technique to fulfill the 'Critique existing solutions' or 'Explain your own solution' steps of Adelson's structure.
